_note: Objective concept questions from the inventory's Concepts items, answered from the textbook. wrong = plausible incorrect answers.

items.q: Why did the résumé study vary applicants' names instead of their race?
items.a: Race cannot be manipulated, but names manipulate employers' perception of race while everything else on the résumé stays identical.
wrong: Names were cheaper to change than photographs.
Employers are legally required to ignore names.
Varying names makes the sample representative of all job seekers.

items.q: Why does the mean of a 0/1 variable equal a proportion?
items.a: Summing 0/1 values counts the 1s; dividing by n gives the share of observations equal to 1.
wrong: Because R converts binary variables to percentages automatically.
Because the mean of any variable is always between 0 and 1.
Because the median and mean coincide for binary variables.

items.q: A callback rate falls from 0.097 to 0.064. How big is the difference?
items.a: About 3.2 percentage points (a relative drop of about a third).
wrong: About 3.2 percent.
About 33 percentage points.
About 0.32 percentage points.

items.q: What can a lower callback rate for black-sounding names show, and what can't it show?
items.a: It shows identical résumés are treated differently by race (discrimination), but not whether the discrimination is intentional.
wrong: It proves employers intentionally discriminate.
It shows nothing causal because the study is observational.
It shows racial gaps in education cause the difference.

items.q: Why can't we estimate an individual unit's causal effect directly?
items.a: Only one of its two potential outcomes is ever observed; the other is counterfactual.
wrong: Individual outcomes are measured with too much error.
Individual effects are always zero on average.
Causal effects are only defined for groups, never individuals.

items.q: In a potential-outcomes table, what determines which cell is observed for unit i?
items.a: The unit's treatment status \(T_i\): we see \(Y_i(1)\) if \(T_i = 1\) and \(Y_i(0)\) if \(T_i = 0\).
wrong: The researcher's choice after seeing the data.
Whichever potential outcome is larger.
The unit's pretreatment covariates.

items.q: Why are pretreatment characteristics (like age or education on a résumé) unaffected by the treatment?
items.a: They are determined before treatment is assigned, so manipulating the treatment cannot change them.
wrong: Because researchers hold them fixed by law.
Because they are always randomly assigned.
Because they are measured after the outcome.

items.q: What does 'no causation without manipulation' express?
items.a: Causal questions are hard to define for things that cannot be manipulated, such as immutable characteristics.
wrong: Only laboratory experiments can establish causation.
Correlation implies causation once you manipulate the data.
Every variable in a regression must be manipulated.

items.q: Why is the credibility of any causal estimate tied to identification assumptions?
items.a: Counterfactual outcomes are unobserved, so estimating them always requires assumptions about what would have happened.
wrong: Because statistical software requires assumptions to run.
Because assumptions make the sample larger.
Because assumptions remove measurement error.

items.q: Why is the SATE not directly observable?
items.a: For each group we see outcomes under only one condition; the average outcome under the other condition is missing.
wrong: Because the sample is too small.
Because the SATE is a population quantity, not a sample quantity.
Because outcomes are measured before treatment.

items.q: In the difference-in-means estimator, what stands in for the treated group's missing Y(0)?
items.a: The control group's observed average outcome.
wrong: The treated group's pretreatment outcome.
The overall sample average.
Zero, since untreated outcomes are baseline.

items.q: Randomization makes treatment and control groups identical on average in what?
items.a: All pretreatment characteristics, both observed and unobserved.
wrong: Observed characteristics only.
Their outcomes.
Their treatment effects, exactly, in every sample.

items.q: Which is a threat to an RCT's external validity?
items.a: The study uses a convenience sample of willing volunteers unlike the target population.
wrong: Treatment was randomly assigned.
The control group received no treatment.
Pretreatment covariates are balanced.

items.q: Why do researchers run field experiments rather than lab experiments?
items.a: To make settings and interventions realistic, improving external validity.
wrong: To avoid randomizing treatment.
Because field experiments need no control group.
To increase internal validity at the cost of realism.

items.q: In a randomized experiment, what do small differences in pretreatment covariate means across groups indicate?
items.a: Randomization worked: the groups are balanced, supporting causal interpretation.
wrong: The treatment had no effect.
The sample is representative of the population.
The outcome was measured correctly.

items.q: Why include both a Civic Duty arm and a Neighbors arm in the social pressure study?
items.a: Comparing them isolates the extra effect of social pressure beyond a generic civic appeal.
wrong: To double the sample size.
To check balance on pretreatment covariates.
Because one arm served as a placebo for the other's outcome.

items.q: What is the typical validity trade-off of observational studies relative to RCTs?
items.a: Weaker internal validity (selection bias) but often stronger external validity (real-world settings).
wrong: Stronger internal validity but weaker external validity.
Both stronger internal and external validity.
Identical validity, since both use real data.

items.q: Why did the minimum-wage study check the share of NJ restaurants paying below $5.05 before and after?
items.a: To verify the treatment actually took effect (NJ restaurants complied with the new law).
wrong: To estimate the effect on employment.
To check balance between NJ and PA on unemployment.
To compute the DiD estimate.

items.q: Why must a confounder be a pretreatment variable?
items.a: A variable affected by the treatment is part of the treatment's effect, not a pre-existing difference that biases the comparison.
wrong: Because posttreatment variables cannot be measured.
Because only pretreatment variables are numeric.
Because confounders must be randomly assigned.

items.q: Why is selection bias common in social science?
items.a: People and governments self-select into treatments for reasons related to their outcomes.
wrong: Social scientists always use small samples.
Surveys never ask about treatments.
Randomization is required by law.

items.q: Can confounding ever be fully ruled out in an observational study?
items.a: No; statistical control can reduce it, but unobserved confounders may remain.
wrong: Yes, by controlling for every observed variable.
Yes, with a large enough sample.
Yes, by using the median instead of the mean.

items.q: When subclassifying by chain and then by location gives estimates similar to the overall one, what does that suggest?
items.a: Chain and location are unlikely to be confounding the estimate.
wrong: The treatment has no effect.
Parallel trends hold.
The sample is randomly drawn.

items.q: What data does each design need: cross-section, before-and-after, DiD?
items.a: Cross-section: post-treatment data for both groups. Before-and-after: pre and post for the treated group. DiD: pre and post for both groups.
wrong: All three need pre and post data for both groups.
Cross-section: pre and post for treated; before-and-after: post for both; DiD: post only.
Only DiD needs a control group; the others need only post data.

items.q: The DiD estimate exceeds the before-and-after estimate for NJ. Why?
items.a: The control group (PA) trended downward, and DiD subtracts that trend.
wrong: DiD uses medians instead of means.
NJ had more restaurants than PA.
Before-and-after double-counts the treatment.

items.q: How can researchers make the parallel trends assumption more credible?
items.a: Show that the groups' outcomes moved in parallel over several earlier pre-treatment periods.
wrong: Verify it directly from post-treatment data.
Increase the sample size in the treated group.
Use medians instead of means.

items.q: How does SATT differ from SATE?
items.a: SATT averages causal effects over treated units only; SATE averages over all units in the sample.
wrong: SATT averages over control units only.
SATT uses the median; SATE uses the mean.
They are identical by definition.

items.q: Why is the IQR of NJ wages after the law zero?
items.a: Both the lower and upper quartiles equal the new minimum wage, because many restaurants set wages exactly at $5.05.
wrong: Because no restaurant changed its wage.
Because the IQR is always zero for wages.
Because the maximum equals the minimum.

items.q: Why report median-based DiD estimates alongside mean-based ones?
items.a: As a robustness check: medians are less sensitive to outliers.
wrong: Because DiD requires medians.
Because means are biased in experiments.
To estimate the SATE instead of the SATT.

items.q: The mean change is near 0.02 but the RMS of the change is about 0.30. What does that mean?
items.a: Restaurants changed a lot in both directions; positive and negative changes largely cancel in the mean.
wrong: Most restaurants barely changed.
The RMS is biased upward by the minimum wage.
The data contain an error.

items.q: When does using \(n\) versus \(n-1\) in the standard deviation matter?
items.a: Only in small samples; with enough data the difference is negligible.
wrong: Always; n − 1 gives a completely different scale.
Only for binary variables.
Only when the mean is zero.

items.q: In a joint proportion table of victimization by ISAF and by the Taliban, how do you get the share victimized by ISAF?
items.a: Add the cells in the ISAF = 1 row (harmed by ISAF, whether or not also harmed by the Taliban).
wrong: Read the single cell where both equal 1.
Add the ISAF = 1 column.
Subtract the Taliban row from the ISAF row.

items.q: Why does listwise deletion of the whole data set leave fewer rows than dropping missing values on one variable?
items.a: Listwise deletion drops a respondent missing ANY variable, including ones irrelevant to the analysis.
wrong: Because listwise deletion also removes duplicates.
Because na.omit() removes outliers.
Because the income variable has no missing values.

items.q: Why can a histogram's density exceed 1?
items.a: Density is proportion divided by bin width; with narrow bins the height can exceed 1 while the area stays below 1.
wrong: Because it counts observations, not proportions.
Because density is a percentage.
It cannot; density is always between 0 and 1.

items.q: Why use density rather than frequency when comparing two histograms?
items.a: Density is comparable across distributions with different numbers of observations.
wrong: Frequency cannot show skewness.
Density histograms always have more bins.
Frequency histograms cannot show the median.

items.q: Why set histogram breaks at −0.5, 0.5, 1.5, … for years of education?
items.a: To center each bin on an integer value, so each bar shows the share with exactly that many years.
wrong: To make the histogram symmetric.
Because R cannot use integer breaks.
To hide the respondents with zero years.

items.q: How far do a box plot's whiskers extend?
items.a: To the most extreme data point within 1.5 × IQR of the quartiles (or the min/max if within that range).
wrong: To the minimum and maximum, always.
To 2 standard deviations from the mean.
To the 5th and 95th percentiles.

items.q: When is a histogram more informative than a box plot, and vice versa?
items.a: A histogram shows one distribution's full shape; box plots compare many distributions compactly.
wrong: A histogram compares many groups; a box plot shows one shape.
They always convey the same information.
Box plots show the mean; histograms show the median.

items.q: What does 'representative' mean for a random sample?
items.a: Across repeated samples, sample characteristics equal the population's on average, even if one sample differs by chance.
wrong: Every sample exactly matches the population.
The sample matches the census on age and gender.
The sample contains every type of person.

items.q: What is the parallel between random sampling and random assignment?
items.a: Both use randomization to guarantee balance on observed and unobserved characteristics on average: sample vs population, treatment vs control.
wrong: Both guarantee internal validity.
Both require a control group.
Both remove nonresponse bias.

items.q: Why did the 1948 polls wrongly predict Dewey would beat Truman?
items.a: They used quota sampling, which can match observed quotas but still select respondents unrepresentative on unobserved traits.
wrong: They used simple random samples that were too small.
They used random digit dialing.
Their questions were subject to social desirability bias.

items.q: Why can random digit dialing produce selection bias?
items.a: Some people have no phone and others have several, so selection probabilities are unequal.
wrong: Because phone numbers are not random.
Because it uses quota sampling.
Because it only reaches unit nonrespondents.

items.q: Why log-transform village population?
items.a: Population is right-skewed by a few very large villages; the log reduces the skew.
wrong: To make negative populations positive.
Because population is a factor variable.
To convert counts into proportions.

items.q: What is log base 10 of 1000? Of 0.01?
items.a: 3 and −2.
wrong: 3 and 2.

items.q: Nonresponse to victimization questions is highest in the most violent provinces. Why does that matter?
items.a: Nonresponse is systematic, not random, so analyzing only responders may bias estimates.
wrong: It proves the survey used quota sampling.
It means those provinces should be dropped.
It has no effect because the rate is low.

items.q: In a list experiment, why does no respondent in the Taliban list group answer 0 or 4?
items.a: Answering 0 or 4 would reveal their view of the Taliban (floor/ceiling effects), so they avoid it.
wrong: The list only had three items.
Randomization failed.
Those answers were coded as missing.

items.q: How does the randomized response technique protect respondents?
items.a: A private random device decides whether to answer honestly, so no individual answer reveals the truth, yet known probabilities allow aggregate estimates.
wrong: Respondents answer anonymously online.
Interviewers skip sensitive questions at random.
Respondents report only a count of items.

items.q: Under the spatial voting model, when does a legislator vote against a proposal?
items.a: When their ideal point is closer to the status quo than to the proposal.
wrong: When the proposal is closer to their ideal point.
When their party opposes it, regardless of distance.
When the proposal passes unanimously.

items.q: Why do unanimous votes reveal nothing about legislators' ideology?
items.a: Everyone votes the same way, so the votes cannot distinguish legislators' positions.
wrong: Unanimous votes are never recorded.
They reveal only the second dimension.
They are excluded from DW-NOMINATE by law.

items.q: Polarization and inequality both rose from 1947 to 2013 (correlation ≈ 0.94). Why not conclude inequality causes polarization?
items.a: Many variables trend upward over time (e.g., life expectancy), so a shared trend yields high correlation without causation.
wrong: Because the correlation is negative.
Because the Gini coefficient cannot be correlated with anything.
Because correlation above 0.9 is always spurious.

items.q: What happens to a z-score if x is transformed to \(ax + b\) with \(a > 0\)? With \(a < 0\)?
items.a: With \(a > 0\) it is unchanged; with \(a < 0\) it flips sign (same magnitude).
wrong: It is multiplied by \(a\) in both cases.
It shifts by \(b\) in both cases.
It is unchanged in both cases.

items.q: Why is correlation unchanged if income is measured in thousands of dollars instead of dollars?
items.a: Correlation is built from z-scores, which do not depend on units.
wrong: Because income has no units.
Because R rescales automatically.
It changes by a factor of 1000.

items.q: In a Q-Q plot of Democrats (x) vs Republicans (y), lower quantiles lie ABOVE the 45° line. Meaning?
items.a: At those quantiles Republicans have higher (more conservative) values: liberal Republicans are more conservative than liberal Democrats.
wrong: Democrats are more conservative at every quantile.
The distributions are identical.
Republicans are more dispersed.

items.q: A Q-Q plot's points form a line flatter than 45°. What does that say?
items.a: The distribution on the horizontal axis is more dispersed than the one on the vertical axis.
wrong: The vertical-axis distribution is more dispersed.
The two distributions have the same mean.
The variables are negatively correlated.

items.q: What happens when a data frame with a factor and a numeric column is coerced to a matrix?
items.a: Everything becomes character, since a matrix holds a single type.
wrong: The factor is dropped.
Everything becomes numeric.
R throws an error.

items.q: Why standardize variables before k-means clustering (usually)?
items.a: So the clustering does not depend on each variable's measurement scale.
wrong: So the algorithm converges in one iteration.
Because k-means needs negative values.
To choose the number of clusters automatically.

items.q: Why run k-means with several random starting values (nstart)?
items.a: Results depend on the initial centroids; multiple starts help find a better solution.
wrong: To choose k automatically.
To standardize the data.
Because one start always fails to converge.

items.q: Why is judging a clustering result hard?
items.a: It is unsupervised: there is no outcome variable to check whether clusters are 'correct', so human judgment is needed.
wrong: Because clusters always equal parties.
Because k-means has no objective function.
Because clusters cannot be plotted.

items.q: With k = 2, clusters perfectly match party in the 112th Congress but not the 80th. What does that show?
items.a: Polarization increased: the parties became ideologically distinct groups.
wrong: k-means failed in the 80th Congress.
The 80th Congress had only one party.
The racial dimension became more important.

items.q: How can poll predictions be nearly unbiased yet have an RMSE of about 6 points?
items.a: Large positive and negative errors cancel in the mean, but each individual state's error can still be large.
wrong: Because RMSE ignores large errors.
Because bias and RMSE measure the same thing.
Because the polls were only conducted in six states.

items.q: Treating an Obama win as 'positive', what is a false negative?
items.a: A state predicted to go to McCain that Obama actually won.
wrong: A state predicted for Obama that McCain won.
A state predicted for Obama that Obama won.
A state with no polls.

items.q: On a plot of predicted (x) vs actual (y) margins, where are the wrong-winner states?
items.a: In the upper-left (predicted loss, actual win) and lower-right (predicted win, actual loss) quadrants.
wrong: On the 45-degree line.
Anywhere above the 45-degree line.
In the upper-right and lower-left quadrants.

items.q: Why is there a trade-off between false positives and false negatives?
items.a: Making the classifier call 'positive' less often reduces false positives but increases false negatives, and vice versa.
wrong: Because their sum is always constant.
Because both are measured by RMSE.
There is no trade-off; both can always be zero.

items.q: Why pre-allocate a container like rep(NA, n) before a loop?
items.a: So each iteration can store its result in position i of an existing vector.
wrong: Because loops cannot print output otherwise.
To make the loop run in parallel.
Because NA values speed up arithmetic.

items.q: How does ifelse() differ from if () {} else {}?
items.a: ifelse() works element by element on a vector; if/else chooses which block of code to run based on one condition.
wrong: They are identical.
if/else works on vectors; ifelse() only on single values.
ifelse() cannot return numbers.

items.q: A scatter plot shows a clear U-shape but the correlation is near 0. Why?
items.a: Correlation measures only linear association, which a symmetric nonlinear pattern lacks.
wrong: The variables are independent.
There is an error in the data.
Correlation ignores outliers.

items.q: In \(\hat{Y} = -0.31 + 0.66\,\text{competence}\), how much is the predicted margin expected to change when competence rises by 0.1?
items.a: By about 0.066 (6.6 percentage points).

items.q: What is the difference between the error term \(\varepsilon\) and the residual \(\hat{\varepsilon}\)?
items.a: \(\varepsilon\) is the unobserved deviation from the true line; \(\hat{\varepsilon} = Y - \hat{Y}\) is its estimate from the fitted line.
wrong: They are the same thing.
\(\hat{\varepsilon}\) is the true error; \(\varepsilon\) is its estimate.
\(\varepsilon\) is the difference between \(\hat{Y}\) and \(\bar{Y}\).

items.q: The residuals from a least-squares fit average to zero. Does this mean the linear model is correct?
items.a: No; it is an algebraic property of least squares that holds for any data set.
wrong: Yes; it proves the linear model is correct.
Yes, if the sample is large.
Only when the correlation is 1.

items.q: If correlation is 0.5, what change in Y (in SDs) goes with a 1-SD increase in X?
items.a: 0.5 standard deviations of Y.
wrong: 2 standard deviations of Y.
1 standard deviation of Y.
0.25 standard deviations of Y.

items.q: Students who aced the midterm tend to score lower on the final. What is the textbook explanation?
items.a: Regression towards the mean: extreme scores partly reflect chance, which need not repeat.
wrong: They studied less after doing well.
The final was harder.
Grades converge over time for everyone.

items.q: Why prefer merge() over cbind() to combine two state-level data sets?
items.a: merge() matches rows by a key; cbind() assumes identical row order and can silently misalign units.
wrong: cbind() cannot combine data frames.
merge() is faster for large data.
cbind() drops duplicated columns.

items.q: Why is the intercept zero when both variables in a regression are standardized?
items.a: \(\hat{\alpha} = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}\bar{X}\), and standardized variables have mean zero.
wrong: Because standardization forces the slope to 1.
Because R drops the intercept automatically.
Because the correlation is zero.

items.q: Removing Palm Beach raised \(R^2\) from 0.51 to 0.85. What does that show?
items.a: A single outlier was strongly influencing the fitted line and hurting fit.
wrong: Perot votes cause Buchanan votes.
The model is overfit.
\(R^2\) is not a measure of fit.

items.q: Why is a high in-sample \(R^2\) not a guarantee of good predictions elsewhere?
items.a: The model may be overfit to idiosyncrasies of the sample and predict poorly out of sample.
wrong: Because \(R^2\) is always biased downward.
Because \(R^2\) measures causality.
Because out-of-sample \(R^2\) is always higher.

items.q: Why can't we compare policies in districts that elect women with districts that don't to learn women's effect?
items.a: Districts electing women may differ in other ways (e.g., ideology) that also affect policy: confounding.
wrong: Because women are rarely elected.
Because policy outcomes cannot be measured.
Because the comparison has no control group.

items.q: In lm(water ~ reserved) with reserved coded 0/1, what are the intercept and slope?
items.a: Intercept: mean water in unreserved villages. Slope: difference in means (reserved − unreserved).
wrong: Intercept: overall mean; slope: correlation.
Intercept: reserved-village mean; slope: unreserved mean.
Intercept: difference in means; slope: control mean.

items.q: With a factor predictor and an intercept, why is one level left out?
items.a: It is the base level absorbed into the intercept; including all levels plus an intercept would be redundant.
wrong: Because R drops the level with the fewest observations.
Because that level has no effect.
Because factors can have at most three levels.

items.q: What does removing the intercept (−1) with a factor predictor change?
items.a: Each coefficient becomes a group mean rather than a difference from the base level.
wrong: It changes the fitted values.
It forces all coefficients to zero.
It drops the base level from the data.

items.q: Why never rely on unadjusted \(R^2\) to choose between models with different numbers of predictors?
items.a: Adding any predictor can only lower SSR, so unadjusted \(R^2\) never falls; adjusted \(R^2\) penalizes extra predictors.
wrong: Because unadjusted \(R^2\) can be negative.
Because unadjusted \(R^2\) ignores the intercept.
Because adjusted \(R^2\) is always larger.

items.q: What is the difference between fitted() and predict(newdata = ...)?
items.a: fitted() gives predictions for the data used to fit the model; predict() can predict for new data.
wrong: They are identical in every case.
predict() only works without an intercept.
fitted() returns residuals.

items.q: In \(Y = \alpha + \beta_1\,\text{primary2004} + \beta_2\,\text{Neighbors} + \beta_3(\text{primary2004} \times \text{Neighbors})\), what is the Neighbors effect for 2004 voters?
items.a: \(\beta_2 + \beta_3\).
wrong: \(\beta_1 + \beta_2\).

items.q: In R formulas, what is the difference between x1:x2 and x1*x2?
items.a: x1:x2 is only the interaction term; x1*x2 adds both main effects and the interaction.
wrong: They are identical.
x1*x2 multiplies the variables without an interaction.
x1:x2 includes main effects; x1*x2 does not.

items.q: Why interpret a quadratic interaction model through predict() rather than its coefficients?
items.a: Its coefficients have no simple individual meaning; predicted differences at chosen values are interpretable.
wrong: Because predict() adds a causal interpretation.
Because the coefficients are always zero.
Because lm() cannot fit squared terms.

items.q: What does I(age^2) do inside an lm() formula?
items.a: Tells R to treat ^ arithmetically, adding age squared as a predictor.
wrong: Creates an interaction between age and itself as a factor.
Takes the inverse of age.
Removes the intercept.

items.q: Why compare MPs who barely won with candidates who barely lost?
items.a: Near the threshold, winners and losers should be similar except for holding office, removing confounding.
wrong: Because close races have larger samples.
Because losers never hold office later.
To estimate the effect for all MPs regardless of margin.

items.q: Why use exp() on the RD predictions for Tory wealth?
items.a: The regressions model log wealth; exp() converts predictions back to pounds.
wrong: To make the predictions positive.
To standardize wealth.
Because the margin is in logs.

items.q: In the RD placebo test, the effect on the previous election's margin is about −0.017. What does that suggest?
items.a: The estimate is near zero, supporting the RD design's validity.
wrong: Holding office changed past elections.
The design is invalid.
Tory MPs lose wealth.

items.q: To whom does an RD estimate apply?
items.a: Only to units near the threshold (e.g., candidates in close races).
wrong: To all units in the population.
To units far from the threshold.
Only to the control group.

items.q: An object named Result and another named result: same or different?
items.a: Different: R object names are case-sensitive.
wrong: Same: R ignores case.
Same, but R warns you.
Different only if one is a character.

items.q: Why can seq(to = 2010, by = 10, from = 1950) reorder its arguments freely?
items.a: Named arguments are matched by name, so their order does not matter.
wrong: seq() sorts its inputs automatically.
R always ignores argument order.
Only numeric arguments can be reordered.

items.q: Why does load() need no assignment arrow, unlike read.csv()?
items.a: An RData file stores objects with their names; load() restores them under those names.
wrong: load() only works on CSV files.
load() returns nothing useful.
read.csv() also needs no assignment.

items.q: What does world.pop[-3] do to world.pop?
items.a: Returns the vector without its 3rd element; world.pop itself is unchanged.
wrong: Deletes the 3rd element from world.pop permanently.

items.q: Why does the book advise not saving the workspace automatically when quitting R?
items.a: The hidden .RData file reloads silently, so you lose track of which objects exist; save what you need explicitly.
wrong: Because R deletes saved workspaces.

items.q: How often do you need install.packages() versus library()?
items.a: Install once per computer; load with library() in each session.
wrong: Both every session.
library() once; install every session.
